walkthroughs.body_html:
Hinduism Option — a core area of GCSE Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Hinduism Option brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Hinduism Option.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: How many main avatars of Vishnu?
Who is the destroyer in the Trimurti?
options: Brahma
Vishnu
Shiva
Ganesh
Hinduism worships no gods, only ancestors.
Hinduism is straightforwardly polytheistic with millions of separate gods.
It is more accurately described as henotheistic or monistic — many gods (devas) are considered aspects or manifestations of one ultimate reality (Brahman).
Karma is a god who decides what happens to you.

mcqs.q: What does karma mean in Hindu and Buddhist thought?
options: The principle that actions have moral consequences shaping future experience or rebirth — not fate, but ethical cause and effect built into reality.
Karma is a god who decides what happens to you.
Hinduism worships no gods, only ancestors.
Karma is when bad things happen to bad people as punishment.

mcqs.q: How do samsara, karma and moksha fit together in Hindu thought?
options: Samsara is the cycle of rebirth; karma is the law of action and consequence that drives rebirth; moksha is liberation from samsara — these form a connected chain, not three independent ideas.
Moksha is the Hindu word for heaven.
Hinduism worships no gods, only ancestors.
Samsara, karma and moksha are three separate Hindu deities.
